mainTopic: The machlokes between רבי יוחנן (אשו משום חציו, his fire is like his arrows) and ריש לקיש (אשו משום ממונו, his fire is like his property), tested against the משנה of the burning גדיש with a tied עבד or גדי.
overview: This עמוד tests the מחלוקת between רבי יוחנן, who holds that a person's fire is like his arrows (אשו משום חציו), and ריש לקיש, who holds that it is like his property (אשו משום ממונו). First the גמרא finishes rejecting a proof from the camel-and-lamp case, which depends only on who was careless. Next it brings a משנה: someone who burns a stack with a tied slave is completely exempt. That seems to fit only the arrows view. ריש לקיש answers that he lit the slave's own body, which is murder under every view. The גמרא then explains that this משנה still teaches something new, because the goat and the slave had different owners. A second proof comes from a משנה that exempts someone who sends fire with a חרש, שוטה וקטן. ריש לקיש, quoting חזקיה, limits that משנה to a coal the חרש fanned, while handing over a flame makes the sender liable. רבי יוחנן says even a flame is exempt, unless the sender hands over wood, chips and a lamp. Finally רבא shows that a פסוק supports רבי יוחנן, and he begins quoting a ברייתא that continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: The camel case is really about who was careless
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes pushing off the proof from the camel-and-lamp case. In the first clause the camel owner is liable because he overloaded his camel. In the second clause the storekeeper is liable because he put his lamp outside.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the first part of the case, the camel owner pays, because he should not have loaded so much flax onto the camel. In the second part, the storekeeper pays, because he should not have left his lamp outside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is closing off an earlier attempted proof. It shows that the camel-and-lamp case is decided only by who acted carelessly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone wanted to use this case to decide between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש. The גמרא answers that the ruling has nothing to do with whether fire counts as 'arrows' or 'property.' It simply blames whichever person was negligent, so that proof falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: The first clause of a teaching
The latter clause of a teaching
To overload the cargo
Storekeeper

steps.whatToRemember: The camel-and-lamp case proves nothing about אשו משום חציו or אשו משום ממונו. It is just about who was careless.

phrases.english: In the first clause, the camel owner is liable,
phrases.notes: This goes back to the case of a camel loaded with flax that caught fire from a storekeeper's lamp.

phrases.english: because he should not have
overloaded the cargo.
In the latter clause, the storekeeper is liable,
because he should not have
placed his lamp outside.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the deflection of the earlier camel-and-lamp proof, which began before this section.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects using the camel-and-lamp case as proof for either side of the מחלוקת.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The liability in that case comes from negligence, not from the nature of fire damage.

steps.title: A new proof from the burning stack with a goat and a slave
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה. If a goat was tied to the stack and a slave was next to it, the person who lit the fire is liable. If the slave was tied and the goat was loose, he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: Someone sets fire to a stack of grain. If a goat was tied to it and a slave was standing nearby, and they burned, he must pay. If the slave was tied to it and the goat was nearby, and they burned, he pays nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source to help settle the מחלוקת. This step only presents the משנה; the next step will show how it might cause a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key point is the second case: when the עבד is tied, the person who lit the fire is completely פטור, even for the grain and the goat. The גמרא will look for the reason behind this exemption, because that reason may show how fire damage works.

keyTerms.meaning: A stack of grain
Tied up
Next to, nearby

steps.confusionAlert: In the first case he pays for the stack and the goat, but not for the loose slave. The slave could have run away from the fire.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
One who ignites a stack of grain,
and there was a goat tied to it,
and a slave next to it,
and it was burned with it: he is liable.
If a slave was tied to it,
and a goat next to it,
and it was burned with it: he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the camel proof was rejected, a new source is brought.
steps.raayaObject: Whether fire liability is like one's arrows (רבי יוחנן) or like one's property (ריש לקיש).
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about one who burns a גדיש with a tied עבד, which exempts him completely.

steps.title: The exemption fits the 'arrows' view but seems hard for the 'property' view
steps.stepSummary: According to אשו משום חציו, he is exempt because it is as if he killed the slave himself. According to אשו משום ממונו, why is he exempt? An owner whose ox kills a slave still has to pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: It works well for the one who says fire is like a person's arrows; that is why he is exempt. But for the one who says fire is like a person's property, why is he exempt? If his ox killed a slave, would he also not have to pay?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses the משנה to challenge ריש לקיש. His view seems unable to explain why the person who lit the fire is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If fire is like arrows, burning the tied slave is murder by his own hand. Since he is חייב מיתה, he pays nothing, under the rule of קם ליה בדרבה מיניה. But if fire is only like his property, he did not kill anyone himself, just as when his ox kills. Then he should have to pay, so the exemption looks wrong for ריש לקיש.

keyTerms.meaning: It works well (sets up a contrast with the view that has trouble)
His fire counts as his arrows (direct personal action)
His fire counts as his property (like his animal)
Why?

phrases.english: It works well according to the one who says
his fire is like his arrows:
that is why he is exempt.
But according to the one who says
his fire is like his property,
why is he exempt?
If his ox killed a slave,
phrases.notes: The owner of an ox that kills a slave pays thirty shekels (שמות 21:32).

phrases.english: would he also not be liable?!

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר אִשּׁוֹ מִשּׁוּם חִצָּיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws out the implication of the משנה from step 2 against ריש לקיש.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's view that אשו משום ממונו.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under the 'property' view he did not personally kill, so he should pay, just as when one's ox kills a slave. The משנה's full exemption fits only the 'arrows' view.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: he set fire to the slave's body itself
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש explains that the משנה is talking about someone who lit the slave's own body. That is direct murder, so he gets the death penalty and is exempt from payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש can answer you: What case are we dealing with here? One where he set fire directly to the slave's body. So he is subject to the greater punishment, and he does not pay.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש defends his view by narrowing the case in the משנה. The exemption comes from a direct killing, not from the fire spreading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Lighting a person's body is murder by one's own hand according to everyone. So the death penalty, and with it the exemption from paying, does not depend on calling fire 'arrows.' The משנה no longer proves רבי יוחנן's view.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (introduces a narrowed case)
He set on fire
He receives only the greater punishment (death), so he does not also pay

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common move in the גמרא: a source that seems to back one side is explained as a special case that every opinion agrees with.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לְךָ רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish can say to you:
With what are we dealing here?
Where he set fire to the slave's body itself,
so he is subject to the greater punishment.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לְךָ רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 3 on behalf of ריש לקיש.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The slave died from fire that spread from the stack, so only the 'arrows' view could make it murder.
steps.terutzMaskana: He lit the slave directly, which is murder under every view, so the exemption fits ריש לקיש too.

steps.title: Why would the משנה need to teach something so obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges ריש לקיש's answer. If the משנה is about someone who set the slave himself on fire, it is obvious that he is exempt from paying.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why does the משנה need to say it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on ריש לקיש's answer from Step 4. If the person burned the slave directly, why would the משנה bother to tell us he is exempt?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who directly kills a person is a murderer and gets the death penalty. It is a well-known rule that a person who gets the death penalty for an act does not also pay for that act. So the exemption seems too obvious to be the lesson of a משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: If so; if that is really the case
Why say it? The point seems obvious

phrases.english: If so, what is the point of saying it?
phrases.notes: He means: if the man lit the slave himself, of course he is exempt from paying. He is a murderer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer ריש לקיש gave in Step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's reading that the משנה is about lighting the slave's own body.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If that reading is right, the exemption is obvious, so the משנה would be teaching nothing new.

steps.title: The goat and the slave had different owners
steps.stepSummary: The משנה is needed for the case where the goat belongs to one person and the slave belongs to someone else.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed for a case where the goat belonged to one person and the slave belonged to another.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה teaches something new after all. The goat and the slave belonged to two different owners.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We might have thought he still has to pay the goat's owner, since that person is not the slave's owner. The משנה teaches that one act that brings the death penalty frees him from paying anyone at all for that act, including the owner of the goat.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for this case; the ruling is aimed at a special situation
Belonging to one person; here the goat and the slave each have a different owner

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה about the goat and slave teaches that the death penalty for one act frees a person from paying for everything that act damaged, even when another person owned the property.

phrases.english: No, it is needed only
where the goat belongs to one person and the slave to another.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: two different owners
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the goat's owner is a different person, the arsonist might still have to pay him.
steps.terutzMaskana: The death penalty for this one act frees him from paying anyone for it, so the משנה does teach something new.

steps.title: New proof: sending fire with a חרש, שוטה וקטן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה. Someone who sends fire with a חרש, שוטה, or קטן is exempt in human court but liable in the heavenly court.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: one who sends fire in the hands of a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, or a minor is exempt by human law but liable by the laws of Heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new attempt to settle whether fire is like one's arrows or like one's property. It quotes a משנה about giving fire to people who are not legally responsible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sender is exempt in court even though the fire caused damage. This step only brings the source. The next step will show which view it seems to support.

keyTerms.meaning: A deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, and a minor; people who are not legally responsible
Human law; what a court can make someone pay
The laws of Heaven; a moral duty that a court cannot enforce

phrases.english: Come and hear:
One who sends the fire
in the hand of a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, or a minor
is exempt by human law,
and liable by the laws of Heaven.
phrases.notes: A court can't make him pay, but he still owes it in Heaven's eyes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the goat-and-slave proof was answered, the גמרא tries a new source.
steps.raayaObject: That fire liability is based on אשו משום חציו.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה exempting someone who sends fire with a חרש, שוטה וקטן.

steps.title: This משנה seems to fit only the arrows view
steps.stepSummary: The exemption makes sense if fire is like arrows, because the arrows now belong to the חרש. But if fire is like property, the sender should be liable, just as he would be for handing over his ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for the one who says his fire is like his arrows: these are the arrows of the deaf-mute. But for the one who says his fire is like his property: if he handed his ox to a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, or a minor, would he also not be liable?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the משנה from Step 7 is a problem for the view of אשו משום ממונו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under אשו משום חציו, the fire becomes the חרש's "arrow" once it is in his hand. So the sender did not shoot it, and he is exempt. Under אשו משום ממונו, fire is like an ox the sender owns. An owner who hands his ox to a חרש is still liable, so the משנה's exemption seems to contradict this view.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense; this view has no problem
His fire is like his arrows; he is liable as if he shot it
His fire is like his property; he is liable the way an owner is for his animal

steps.confusionAlert: Under the arrows view, the arrow here belongs to the חרש, not to the sender. That is why the sender is exempt. It is not because nobody caused the fire.

phrases.english: It makes sense according to the one who says
his fire is like his arrows:
these are the deaf-mute's arrows.
But according to the one who says
his fire is like his property:
if he handed over his ox
to a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, or a minor,
would he also not be liable?!

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר אִשּׁוֹ מִשּׁוּם חִצָּיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out how the משנה from Step 7 challenges the property view.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view of אשו משום ממונו.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under the property view, fire should be like an ox. An owner who hands his ox to a חרש is liable, yet the משנה exempts the person who hands over fire.

steps.title: A coal is different from a flame
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש, quoting חזקיה, limits the משנה. The sender is exempt only if he gave a coal and the חרש fanned it. If he gave a flame, he is liable, because the damage is obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was already said about this: ריש לקיש said in the name of חזקיה, they taught this only when he handed him a coal and the deaf-mute fanned it. But if he handed him a flame, he is liable. Why? The damage is obvious.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing the משנה. It is only talking about handing over a coal that the חרש later fanned into a flame.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A coal on its own does not do damage. The חרש is the one who made it dangerous, so the sender is exempt even under the property view. A flame is already dangerous, like handing someone a goring ox, so the sender is liable. Now the משנה fits אשו משום ממונו as well, and the proof falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: It was already said about this; an earlier teaching answers the problem
A glowing coal
He fanned it into a flame
An open flame
The damage is obvious; it is clear harm will follow

steps.whatToRemember: Handing a coal to a חרש, שוטה וקטן makes the sender exempt, because the חרש fanned it. Handing over a flame makes him liable, because the damage is obvious. So this משנה does not prove that fire is like arrows.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule "בָּרִי הֶיזֵּקָא" makes the sender liable when the danger is already clear at the moment he hands it over.

phrases.english: But it was already said about this:
Reish Lakish said in the name of Chizkiya:
They taught this only
when he handed him a coal, and he fanned it;
phrases.notes: The one who fanned it is the חרש, שוטה, or קטן, not the sender.

phrases.english: but if he handed him a flame, he is liable.
What is the reason? The damage is obvious.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 8 and cancels the proof from Step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: coal versus flame
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה exempts anyone who hands fire to a חרש, which would fit only the arrows view.
steps.terutzMaskana: The exemption covers only a coal the חרש fanned. Handing over a flame makes the sender liable, which fits the property view too.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: even a flame is exempt
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says that even if the sender gave the חרש a flame, the sender is exempt. The חרש's handling is what causes the damage. He is liable only if he hands over chopped wood, kindling chips, and a lamp.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן says: even if he gave a flame, he is exempt. He holds that it is the חרש's handling that causes the fire. The sender is not liable until he hands him chopped wood, kindling chips, and a lamp.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives רבי יוחנן's way of reading the משנה about sending fire with a חרש. It is a different approach from the one ריש לקיש gave in the last step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש drew the line between a coal and a flame. רבי יוחנן says even a flame is not enough, because the fire still has to be carried and handled by the חרש. Only when the sender provides a complete fire setup is the damage so certain that it counts as if he started the blaze himself, just like shooting his own arrow.

keyTerms.meaning: An open flame
Exempt from paying
Handling (literally tongs); here, the חרש's handling of the fire
Chopped wood
Kindling chips
A lamp

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two views. ריש לקיש makes the sender liable for a flame. רבי יוחנן exempts him even for a flame, and makes him liable only when he hands over wood, chips, and a lamp together.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan says:
Even if he gave a flame, he is exempt,
because he holds: it is the deaf-mute's handling that causes the fire;
he is not liable until he hands him
chopped wood, kindling chips, and a lamp.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ שַׁלְהֶבֶת – פָּטוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבי יוחנן's different limit on the משנה, set against ריש לקיש's coal-versus-flame line in step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sending fire with a חרש is exempt even with a flame. Liability starts only when wood, chips, and a lamp are all handed over.

steps.title: רבא: the verse supports רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: רבא says a פסוק and a ברייתא both support רבי יוחנן. He explains the פסוק first. It says the fire 'breaks out' on its own, yet it still blames 'the one who ignited it.' This shows that a person's fire counts like his arrows.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: a פסוק and a ברייתא support רבי יוחנן. The פסוק is: 'If fire breaks out.' That means it breaks out on its own. Yet it says, 'the one who ignited the fire shall pay.' Learn from this that his fire is treated like his arrows.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא brings support for רבי יוחנן's basic view that אשו משום חציו. He starts with the proof from the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק seems to contradict itself. First the fire spreads by itself, then the person who lit it must pay. The answer is that the Torah treats the spreading fire as if the person himself did it, like an arrow he shot. That is exactly רבי יוחנן's view.

keyTerms.meaning: A פסוק from the Torah
A ברייתא, a teaching of the תנאים outside the משנה
The one who lit the fire
His fire counts like his arrows, as a direct act of his
Learn from it; conclude

steps.whyThisMatters: This proof is the basic source for treating fire damage as the person's own direct act, and not only as damage done by his property.

phrases.english: Rava said:

phrases.aramaic: קְרָא וּמַתְנִיתָא מְסַיַּיע לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן.
phrases.english: A verse and a baraita support Rabbi Yochanan.
The verse: as it is written, "If fire breaks out"
meaning it breaks out on its own,
yet "the one who ignited the fire shall pay"
Conclude from this: his fire counts like his arrows.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: קְרָא וּמַתְנִיתָא מְסַיַּיע לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי יוחנן's basic view that fire is like arrows.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's position that אשו משום חציו
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות 22:5, which says the fire goes out by itself yet makes the person who lit it pay

steps.title: רבא begins the baraita proof
steps.stepSummary: רבא starts quoting the ברייתא that also supports רבי יוחנן. It begins with 'The verse opened...'
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא is as it was taught: 'The פסוק opened...'
steps.whatsHappening: This line sets up the second proof, the ברייתא. The quote continues on the next עמוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא promised two supports, a פסוק and a ברייתא. The פסוק is done. Now he opens the ברייתא, whose full point comes once the quote is finished.

keyTerms.meaning: The פסוק opened (began its wording) with

phrases.english: The baraita: as it is taught:
The verse opened

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the second of the two supports רבא promised.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's position that אשו משום חציו
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about how the פסוק on fire damage begins and ends
